sectionTitle: Carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases

specStatements.text: Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
Students should be able to describe the greenhouse effect in terms of the interaction of short and long wavelength radiation with matter.
Some human activities increase the amounts of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. These include:
carbon dioxide
methane.
Students should be able to recall two human activities that increase the amounts of each of the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane.

Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe that human activities will cause the temperature of the Earth’s atmosphere to increase at the surface and that this will result in global climate change.

However, it is difficult to model such complex systems as global climate change. This leads to simplified models, speculation and opinions presented in the media that may be based on only parts of the evidence and which may be biased.
Students should be able to:
evaluate the quality of evidence in a report about global climate change given appropriate information
describe uncertainties in the evidence base
recognise the importance of peer review of results and of communicating results to a wide range of audiences.
An increase in average global temperature is a major cause of climate change.
There are several potential effects of global climate change.
Students should be able to:
describe briefly four potential effects of global climate change
discuss the scale, risk and environmental implications of global climate change.
The carbon footprint is the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
The carbon footprint can be reduced by reducing emissions of carbon dioxide and methane.
Students should be able to:
describe actions to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and methane
give reasons why actions may be limited.

scopeNotes.statement: Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the three gases the specification names are taught as greenhouse gases. No further greenhouse gases (nitrous oxide, CFCs) are introduced, and the section is not extended into ozone depletion or acid rain. Sulfur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen and carbon monoxide appear only inside corrected distractors, never as taught greenhouse gases.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to describe the greenhouse effect in terms of the interaction of short and long wavelength radiation with matter.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The greenhouse effect is treated qualitatively, in the specification's own terms of short and long wavelength radiation interacting with matter. No named regions of the electromagnetic spectrum beyond 'short' and 'long' wavelength are required, no wavelength values are quoted, and no molecular vibration or bond-absorption mechanism is introduced.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to recall two human activities that increase the amounts of each of the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Recall is limited to two human activities for each gas. Questions ask for activities that belong to the right gas rather than for exhaustive lists, and no emission figures, percentages or country data are required to be remembered.

scopeNotes.statement: However, it is difficult to model such complex systems as global climate change.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Climate modelling is handled qualitatively: students judge why a complex system forces simplification and why media accounts may be partial or biased. No climate model is described in detail, and no calculation or interpretation of model output is required.

scopeNotes.statement: describe briefly four potential effects of global climate change
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Effects are described briefly only. Questions ask students to identify and outline potential effects such as sea level rise, flooding, extreme weather, changes to rainfall patterns and shifts in species distribution; detailed mechanisms, regional projections and numerical predictions are not required.

scopeNotes.statement: The carbon footprint is the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The carbon footprint is treated as a definition to apply, not a quantity to compute. No carbon footprint calculation, no emission factors and no life cycle assessment data handling are asked for anywhere in this section.

concepts.definition: A gas in the atmosphere that absorbs long wavelength radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and re-radiates some of it back towards the Earth. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
The specification names water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). Nitrogen and oxygen, which together make up about 99% of the air, are not greenhouse gases.
The process by which greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life. Without it the Earth's surface would be far colder.
Radiation from the Sun. Most of it passes through the atmosphere without being absorbed by greenhouse gases and is absorbed by the Earth's surface, warming it.
Radiation emitted by the warmed Earth's surface. Its wavelength is longer than that of the radiation arriving from the Sun, and greenhouse gases absorb it.
Greenhouse gases absorb long wavelength radiation from the Earth and re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the surface, so the surface stays warmer.
Burning fossil fuels (in power stations, vehicles and homes) and deforestation, which leaves fewer trees to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Cattle and other livestock farming, and the decay of organic waste in landfill sites. Growing rice in flooded paddy fields also releases methane.
Checking of a scientist's methods, data and conclusions by other scientists working in the same field before the work is published.
The evidence for climate change does not fix a single exact outcome: measurements have limits, the climate system is complex and future emissions are unknown, so predictions are given as ranges.
A report presents only part of the evidence, or presents opinion or speculation as if it were established evidence, often to support a particular point of view.
A long-term change in the Earth's climate, caused mainly by an increase in the average global temperature of the atmosphere at the surface.
Sea level rise and flooding of low-lying land, more frequent and severe storms, changes to the amount and distribution of rainfall, and changes to the range of many wild species.
Risk combines how likely an effect is with how severe it would be. Climate change is global in scale, so the effects and the risks are not confined to the countries that emit the most.
The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
Every stage from obtaining raw materials, through manufacture, transport and use, to disposal at the end of the product's useful life.
Using renewable energy or nuclear power, increasing energy efficiency, carbon capture and storage, carbon taxes and licences, and capturing methane from landfill and livestock.
Cost, the slow pace of scientific and technological development, disagreement between governments, lack of public information and education, and reluctance to change lifestyles.

misconceptions.question: Would the Earth be better off with no greenhouse gases at all?
misconceptions.correct: No. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life; the concern is the extra amount added by human activity.
misconceptions.misconception: The greenhouse effect is simply pollution, so removing all greenhouse gases would be good.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'greenhouse' is almost always met in news reports about global warming, so it becomes attached to harm, and the natural effect that keeps the Earth warm enough to live on is never met.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the natural greenhouse effect, which supports life, from the enhanced effect caused by rising amounts of carbon dioxide and methane.

misconceptions.question: Do greenhouse gases protect us from ultraviolet radiation?
misconceptions.correct: No. That is the job of the ozone layer. Greenhouse gases absorb long wavelength radiation emitted by the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Greenhouse gases form a shield that blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The greenhouse effect and the hole in the ozone layer are met at the same time and both involve gases high in the atmosphere, so the two stories merge.
misconceptions.correction: Ozone depletion and the greenhouse effect are separate: one is about ultraviolet radiation being blocked, the other about long wavelength radiation being absorbed and re-radiated.

misconceptions.question: Is water vapour a greenhouse gas?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The specification names water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases.
misconceptions.misconception: Water vapour is natural and harmless, so it cannot be a greenhouse gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate greenhouse gases with pollution from human activity, and water vapour does not feel like a pollutant, so it is dropped from the list.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the three named gases as a set: water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane. Being natural does not stop a gas absorbing long wavelength radiation.

misconceptions.question: Do greenhouse gases make up most of the atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: No. Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99% of the air; the greenhouse gases are present in much smaller amounts.
misconceptions.misconception: A gas can only have a large warming effect if there is a large amount of it in the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that a big effect needs a big cause, and are rarely shown how small the carbon dioxide and methane fractions of the atmosphere actually are.
misconceptions.correction: A small amount of gas can have a large effect because each molecule absorbs long wavelength radiation; amount and effect are not proportional in a simple way.

misconceptions.question: Which radiation do greenhouse gases absorb?
misconceptions.correct: They absorb the long wavelength radiation emitted by the warmed surface of the Earth.
misconceptions.misconception: Greenhouse gases absorb the short wavelength radiation arriving from the Sun.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Sun is the obvious source of heat, so students assume the atmosphere must be absorbing sunlight rather than radiation emitted back out by the ground.
misconceptions.correction: Track the two steps: short wavelength radiation passes through and warms the surface; the surface then emits long wavelength radiation, which greenhouse gases absorb.

misconceptions.question: Do greenhouse gases reflect radiation back to Earth?
misconceptions.correct: No. They absorb long wavelength radiation and then re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: The layer of greenhouse gases acts like a mirror that reflects radiation straight back down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook arrows curving back to the ground look like reflection, and reflection is the easier idea to picture, so absorption and re-radiation are skipped.
misconceptions.correction: Use the words the specification uses: the radiation is absorbed by the gas and then re-radiated, not bounced off a surface.

misconceptions.question: Does the atmosphere trap warm air like a blanket?
misconceptions.correct: No. The greenhouse effect is about radiation being absorbed and re-radiated, not about warm air being physically held in.
misconceptions.misconception: Greenhouse gases stop hot air escaping, the way a blanket or a glass greenhouse does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The greenhouse analogy is taught first and taken literally; a real greenhouse works mainly by stopping convection, which is a different mechanism.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the effect in terms of radiation: short wavelength in, long wavelength absorbed and re-radiated. The blanket picture explains the wrong mechanism.

misconceptions.question: Is deforestation a problem because trees give out carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. Trees remove carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis, so cutting them down leaves less carbon dioxide being taken out.
misconceptions.misconception: Trees release carbon dioxide, so cutting them down should lower the amount in the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that plants respire and release carbon dioxide, and forget that over a growing tree's life photosynthesis removes far more than respiration returns.
misconceptions.correction: Deforestation raises atmospheric carbon dioxide in two ways: less is removed by photosynthesis, and burning or decay of the felled wood releases more.

misconceptions.question: Is cattle farming a source of carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Cattle farming is named as a source of methane. The named carbon dioxide activities are burning fossil fuels and deforestation.
misconceptions.misconception: Any human activity that adds a greenhouse gas must be adding carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide dominates the news coverage, so every source gets filed under it and methane sources are never learned separately.
misconceptions.correction: Keep two short lists: carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels and deforestation; methane from cattle farming and decay of waste in landfill sites.

misconceptions.question: Does burning coal in a power station release methane?
misconceptions.correct: No. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide. Methane comes from cattle and from decaying waste in landfill.
misconceptions.misconception: Burning fuels releases every kind of greenhouse gas, including methane.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Combustion is treated as a single 'pollution' event, so all the gases a student has heard of get attached to it.
misconceptions.correction: Match each activity to its gas. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel produces carbon dioxide and water, not methane.

misconceptions.question: Have scientists proved that human activity causes climate change?
misconceptions.correct: Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe human activities will raise the surface temperature and cause global climate change.
misconceptions.misconception: Science proves things beyond all doubt, so either it is proved or there is no evidence at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Proof' is used loosely in everyday speech and in mathematics, so students expect scientific claims to be certain rather than well evidenced.
misconceptions.correction: Use the specification's own wording: based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe. Evidence can be strong without being called proof.

misconceptions.question: If scientists disagree about details, is the evidence worthless?
misconceptions.correct: No. Disagreement about the size and timing of effects sits alongside a large body of peer-reviewed evidence that the surface temperature is rising.
misconceptions.misconception: Because some scientists disagree, nothing about climate change can be relied on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Media coverage stages the topic as a two-sided debate, which makes uncertainty about detail look like uncertainty about everything.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the well-evidenced core from the uncertain detail; uncertainty in predictions is normal in a complex system.

misconceptions.question: Are climate models just opinion?
misconceptions.correct: No. Models are built from measured data. Because global climate is very complex, models have to be simplified, which is why predictions vary.
misconceptions.misconception: A model is only a guess, so climate predictions are no better than opinions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'model' suggests something made up, and students rarely see the measured data a climate model is built from.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says complex systems are difficult to model, which leads to simplified models. Simplified is not the same as invented.

misconceptions.question: Does 'biased' mean the measurements were wrong?
misconceptions.correct: No. A biased report presents only part of the evidence, or presents opinion as evidence, to favour a point of view.
misconceptions.misconception: Bias is an error in the instruments or in the way the data were collected.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Bias' has a technical meaning in measurement work, and students transfer it to reporting without noticing the change of meaning.
misconceptions.correction: In this section bias is about selection and presentation of evidence in the media, not about the accuracy of a thermometer.

misconceptions.question: Does 'uncertainty' mean the scientists made mistakes?
misconceptions.correct: No. Uncertainty describes the range within which a value or prediction lies, given the limits of the data and the complexity of the system.
misconceptions.misconception: Uncertainty in the evidence base means the scientists got their measurements wrong.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech being uncertain means not knowing, which sounds like incompetence rather than an honest statement of limits.
misconceptions.correction: Uncertainty is reported precisely because the work is careful: it states how far predictions may range, and why.

misconceptions.question: Is a single weather station over two years good evidence about global climate?
misconceptions.correct: No. Global claims need measurements from many places over decades, because weather varies far more from year to year than climate does.
misconceptions.misconception: Real measured data is good evidence whatever the sample size or time period.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge evidence by whether it was measured rather than by whether the sample and time span match the claim being made.
misconceptions.correction: Evaluate evidence against the claim: a global, long-term claim needs global, long-term data.

misconceptions.question: Does peer review make a result certain?
misconceptions.correct: No. Peer review means other scientists have checked the methods and conclusions before publication; the result can still be revised later.
misconceptions.misconception: Once work is peer reviewed it is proved correct and cannot be questioned again.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Peer review is introduced as a quality check, and students round 'checked' up to 'certain'.
misconceptions.correction: Peer review raises confidence and filters out poor work; later evidence can still change the conclusion.

misconceptions.question: Is melting polar ice a cause of climate change?
misconceptions.correct: It is a potential effect of rising average global temperature, not one of the human activities that cause it.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting ice caps are one of the human activities that increase greenhouse gases.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Causes and effects appear in the same paragraph of most revision notes, and melting ice is the image most strongly linked to the topic.
misconceptions.correction: Sort the topic into causes (human activities releasing carbon dioxide and methane) and effects (sea level rise, flooding, extreme weather, species changes).

misconceptions.question: Is acid rain an effect of global climate change?
misconceptions.correct: No. Acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen, and belongs to a different part of the specification.
misconceptions.misconception: Acid rain and ozone damage are among the potential effects of climate change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All the atmospheric pollution topics are taught close together, so their effects get pooled into one list.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the effects of climate change separate: sea level rise, flooding, extreme weather, changed rainfall patterns and changes to species distribution.

misconceptions.question: Does a 1 °C rise in average global temperature mean every day is 1 °C warmer?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is an average across the whole Earth and across the year; local changes may be much larger or smaller.
misconceptions.misconception: A small rise in the average is too small to matter, because daily temperatures vary far more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the average with the day-to-day range they experience, which is much bigger, and conclude the rise is trivial.
misconceptions.correction: A shift in the global average moves the whole distribution, which changes ice cover, sea level and the frequency of extreme weather.

misconceptions.question: Is the carbon footprint just the carbon dioxide given off when a product is made?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the total carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of the product, service or event.
misconceptions.misconception: The carbon footprint only counts the carbon dioxide released during manufacture.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Manufacture is the stage students picture first, and 'full life cycle' is easy to read past in the definition.
misconceptions.correction: Include every stage: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal, and include methane as well as carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: Is the carbon footprint the mass of carbon inside the product?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is an amount of greenhouse gas emitted, not carbon contained in the object.
misconceptions.misconception: A product's carbon footprint is the amount of carbon it is made of.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'carbon' in the name points at the material, and 'footprint' is a vague enough word to let that reading stand.
misconceptions.correction: Read the definition as written: the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle.

misconceptions.question: Can filters on a chimney remove greenhouse gases?
misconceptions.correct: Filters and scrubbers are used to remove sulfur dioxide and particulates. Reducing carbon dioxide needs less fuel burned or carbon capture and storage.
misconceptions.misconception: Fitting a filter to a chimney will stop the carbon dioxide escaping.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Flue gas desulfurisation is taught nearby, so the same fix is assumed to work for every gas leaving a chimney.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon dioxide is a product of combustion itself, so it is reduced by burning less fuel, switching fuel or capturing and storing the gas.

misconceptions.question: Are actions to cut emissions limited because there is no evidence?
misconceptions.correct: No. The limits are practical: cost, slow technological development, disagreement between governments, and reluctance to change lifestyles.
misconceptions.misconception: Emissions are not cut because scientists have not shown that they cause warming.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Media framing of the topic as an unsettled argument is carried over into the reasons why action is slow.
misconceptions.correction: Give practical reasons: cost, the pace of scientific and technological development, lack of international agreement, and lack of public information.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about greenhouse gases in the Earth's atmosphere is correct?

options.text: Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are all greenhouse gases.
options.rationale: These are the three greenhouse gases the specification names.

options.text: Water vapour is a natural gas and so is not a greenhouse gas.
options.rationale: Students link greenhouse gases to pollution, and water vapour does not feel like a pollutant.

options.text: Only gases released by human activity act as greenhouse gases.
options.rationale: Treating the greenhouse effect as pollution makes the gases seem man-made.

options.text: Greenhouse gases make up most of the atmosphere by volume.
options.rationale: A large effect is assumed to need a large amount of gas; in fact nitrogen and oxygen dominate.

mcqs.stem: What do greenhouse gases in the atmosphere do for living things on Earth?

options.text: They block the ultraviolet radiation coming from the Sun.
options.rationale: The ozone layer story is merged with the greenhouse effect.

options.text: They supply the oxygen that living organisms need for respiration.
options.rationale: Any 'useful gas' role is attached to greenhouse gases once they are known to matter.

options.text: They cool the Earth by reflecting sunlight into space.
options.rationale: Reflection is the easier picture, and it is applied in the wrong direction.

options.text: They keep temperatures on Earth high enough to support life.
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification says greenhouse gases maintain.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the greenhouse effect?

options.text: Long wavelength radiation passes through and short wavelength is absorbed.
options.rationale: The two wavelengths are swapped because the Sun is assumed to be what the gases absorb.

options.text: Greenhouse gases reflect the incoming radiation back down to the ground.
options.rationale: Absorption and re-radiation are replaced by simple reflection.

options.text: Short wavelength radiation passes through; long wavelength is absorbed.
options.rationale: Solar radiation passes through the atmosphere, and the long wavelength radiation emitted by the surface is absorbed by greenhouse gases.

options.text: Greenhouse gases hold warm air near the ground, like a blanket.
options.rationale: The greenhouse analogy is taken literally, giving a convection mechanism.

mcqs.stem: Radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground. What happens next?

options.text: The ground reflects the radiation back at the same wavelength.
options.rationale: Reflection is substituted for absorption followed by emission.

options.text: The warmed surface emits longer wavelength radiation.
options.rationale: The Earth's surface, being much cooler than the Sun, radiates at longer wavelengths.

options.text: The surface emits radiation of an even shorter wavelength.
options.rationale: Students assume warming shortens the wavelength, reversing the correct change.

options.text: The warm air rises and is trapped by greenhouse gases.
options.rationale: The blanket picture describes convection rather than radiation.

mcqs.stem: What do greenhouse gases do with the long wavelength radiation they absorb?

options.text: They re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the Earth.
options.rationale: Absorption is followed by re-radiation, and the part sent downwards keeps the surface warm.

options.text: They reflect all of it straight back down to the Earth's surface.
options.rationale: Reflection is easier to picture than absorption and re-radiation.

options.text: They store it permanently, so the energy never leaves the gas.
options.rationale: 'Trapping' is read as energy being held for good.

options.text: They convert it into short wavelength radiation from the Sun.
options.rationale: The two wavelengths are confused, so the change is put the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: Which human activity increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: Growing rice in fields that are kept flooded all year.
options.rationale: A real greenhouse gas source, but it releases methane, not carbon dioxide.

options.text: Keeping large herds of cattle on grassland.
options.rationale: Livestock farming is the named methane activity, not a carbon dioxide one.

options.text: Burying more household waste in landfill sites.
options.rationale: Decay of waste in landfill releases methane, so the gas is misattributed.

options.text: Burning fossil fuels in power stations and vehicles.
options.rationale: Combustion of fossil fuels is a named human source of carbon dioxide.

mcqs.stem: Explain why cutting down large areas of forest increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the air.

options.text: Trees give out carbon dioxide, so cutting them down helps the air.
options.rationale: Respiration is remembered and photosynthesis is forgotten, reversing the argument.

options.text: Cutting the trees down releases the methane that is stored in wood.
options.rationale: The wrong greenhouse gas is attached to the activity.

options.text: Fewer trees are left to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
options.rationale: Photosynthesis is the process that takes carbon dioxide out of the air, so removing trees reduces it.

options.text: Losing trees thins the ozone layer and lets more heat in.
options.rationale: Ozone depletion is confused with the greenhouse effect.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of human activities both increase the amount of methane in the atmosphere?

options.text: Landfill sites and burning of coal.
options.rationale: Landfill is right, but burning coal releases carbon dioxide.

options.text: Cattle farming and rice growing.
options.rationale: Livestock and flooded rice fields are both named methane sources.

options.text: Deforestation and cattle farming.
options.rationale: Cattle are right, but deforestation is a carbon dioxide activity.

options.text: Aerosol sprays and air conditioning.
options.rationale: Ozone layer chemistry is imported into the greenhouse gas topic.

mcqs.stem: A student is asked to name two human activities that increase the amount of carbon dioxide. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Burning fossil fuels for electricity, and deforestation.
options.rationale: These are the two carbon dioxide activities named in the specification.

options.text: Cattle farming, and decay of waste in landfill sites.
options.rationale: Both of these are methane activities, not carbon dioxide ones.

options.text: Burning fossil fuels, and keeping herds of cattle.
options.rationale: Only the first belongs to carbon dioxide; cattle release methane.

options.text: Deforestation, and the melting of the polar ice.
options.rationale: An effect of climate change is listed as if it were a cause.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes what scientists say about human activity and the Earth's temperature?

options.text: Scientists have now proved that human activity is the only possible cause of warming.
options.rationale: Strong evidence is upgraded to proof, and other influences are ruled out.

options.text: Scientists disagree with each other, so there is no reliable evidence at all.
options.rationale: Disagreement about detail is read as the absence of any evidence.

options.text: The claim comes from opinions in the media rather than from measured data.
options.rationale: Media coverage is mistaken for the source of the science itself.

options.text: Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists expect the Earth's surface to warm.
options.rationale: This is the specification's own statement of the scientific position.

mcqs.stem: Why do different climate models give different predictions for future temperatures?

options.text: Climate models are built on opinion rather than on any real measured data.
options.rationale: The word 'model' is read as guesswork.

options.text: The temperature of the whole of the atmosphere cannot be measured well.
options.rationale: Uncertainty in predictions is confused with an inability to measure.

options.text: Global climate is a very complex system, so models must be simplified.
options.rationale: The specification says such complex systems are difficult to model, which leads to simplified models.

options.text: The results of the models have not been checked by peer review.
options.rationale: Peer review is offered as the explanation for any disagreement.

mcqs.stem: A newspaper article about climate change is described as biased. What does this mean?

options.text: Its thermometers were badly calibrated.
options.rationale: The measurement meaning of bias is transferred to reporting.

options.text: It presents only part of the evidence.
options.rationale: Bias here is selective use of evidence, or opinion presented as evidence.

options.text: It quotes peer-reviewed research papers.
options.rationale: Peer review is treated as the thing that makes a report suspect.

options.text: Its writer is uncertain about the outcome.
options.rationale: Uncertainty and bias are treated as the same fault.

mcqs.stem: A website claims that the world is cooling, using two years of readings from one weather station. What is the best evaluation of this evidence?

options.text: The sample is too small and the period too short to show a global trend.
options.rationale: A global, long-term claim needs data from many places over many years.

options.text: The evidence is strong because real temperatures were measured.
options.rationale: Evidence is judged by whether it was measured, not by whether it fits the claim.

options.text: The evidence is worthless because a website is not a journal.
options.rationale: Where it was published replaces any judgement of the data itself.

options.text: Two years is enough if the thermometer was accurate enough.
options.rationale: Accuracy of one instrument is confused with adequacy of the sample.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a genuine uncertainty in the evidence base for global climate change?

options.text: Nobody had measured the temperature of the Earth before the year 2000.
options.rationale: Uncertainty is imagined as a complete absence of past data.

options.text: Scientists made mistakes when they recorded their measurements.
options.rationale: Uncertainty is read as error on the part of the scientists.

options.text: It is not known whether carbon dioxide absorbs radiation.
options.rationale: Settled physics is presented as if it were an open question.

options.text: Future emissions are not known, so predictions are given as a range.
options.rationale: What humans will emit in future is a real unknown, so models give ranges.

mcqs.stem: Why is peer review of climate research important?

options.text: It proves that the conclusions are right and settles the matter for good.
options.rationale: A quality check is upgraded to certainty.

options.text: It lets the general public vote on which scientific results to believe.
options.rationale: Public debate in the media is confused with scientific review.

options.text: Other scientists check the methods and conclusions before publication.
options.rationale: Peer review is checking by other scientists in the same field.

options.text: It keeps the results secret until a government approves them.
options.rationale: Review before publication is read as censorship.

mcqs.stem: Why is a rise of about one degree in the average global temperature important?

options.text: Every place on Earth is now one degree warmer.
options.rationale: An average is read as the same change everywhere.

options.text: It shifts the climate of the whole Earth.
options.rationale: An average across the whole planet moving is a large change to the climate system.

options.text: It is too small to change the weather at all.
options.rationale: The average is compared with the much larger daily range.

options.text: It shows that the ozone layer is thinning.
options.rationale: Ozone depletion is offered as the meaning of warming.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a potential effect of global climate change?

options.text: Sea level rise, causing flooding of low-lying land.
options.rationale: Rising sea level and flooding are named potential effects.

options.text: More acid rain falling on lakes and forests.
options.rationale: Acid rain belongs to sulfur dioxide, not to climate change.

options.text: A larger hole in the ozone layer each spring.
options.rationale: Ozone depletion is a separate atmospheric problem.

options.text: A steady fall in the atmospheric carbon dioxide.
options.rationale: A cause is listed as an effect, and in the wrong direction.

mcqs.stem: Which list contains only potential effects of global climate change?

options.text: Flooding, deforestation, more frequent storms and stronger winds.
options.rationale: Deforestation is a cause of climate change, not an effect of it.

options.text: Rising sea level, acid rain, changes to rainfall patterns.
options.rationale: Acid rain is a different pollution problem.

options.text: Extreme weather, cattle farming, loss of some habitats.
options.rationale: Cattle farming is a methane source, so a cause has been listed.

options.text: Flooding, more extreme weather, changes to species distribution.
options.rationale: All three are potential effects the specification expects students to describe.

mcqs.stem: A report says that the risk to a coastal city from climate change is high. What does describing the risk involve?

options.text: Only how many years it will be before the flooding happens.
options.rationale: Risk is reduced to timing alone.

options.text: Only how many people believe that the report is correct.
options.rationale: Opinion is substituted for likelihood and severity.

options.text: How likely the flooding is, and how severe it would be.
options.rationale: Risk combines the chance of an event with the size of its consequences.

options.text: Only the cost of the sea wall the city must build.
options.rationale: The cost of the response replaces the risk itself.

mcqs.stem: What is the carbon footprint of a product?

options.text: Carbon dioxide given off while the product is made.
options.rationale: Only the manufacturing stage is counted, and only one gas.

options.text: Greenhouse gases emitted over its full life cycle.
options.rationale: The definition covers carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases across the whole life cycle.

options.text: The mass of carbon that the finished object contains.
options.rationale: Carbon in the material is confused with gas emitted.

options.text: The carbon dioxide released while the product is used.
options.rationale: Only the use stage is counted, so the life cycle is cut short.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a carbon footprint is correct?

options.text: It includes methane as well as carbon dioxide, at every stage.
options.rationale: The definition covers carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, over the full life cycle.

options.text: It counts carbon dioxide only, from the factory stage.
options.rationale: Other greenhouse gases and other stages are left out.

options.text: It is the carbon locked inside the finished product.
options.rationale: The name is read as the material rather than the emissions.

options.text: It counts only the gases given off during its transport.
options.rationale: One stage of the life cycle stands in for all of them.

mcqs.stem: A company wants to reduce the carbon footprint of its factory. Which action would do this?

options.text: Fit filters to the chimneys to trap all the carbon dioxide.
options.rationale: Flue gas desulfurisation is assumed to work for carbon dioxide.

options.text: Measure the carbon dioxide released at every stage.
options.rationale: Measuring a footprint is confused with reducing it.

options.text: Move the factory to a country that is much colder.
options.rationale: Location is confused with emissions; nothing about the total changes.

options.text: Take the factory's electricity from wind and solar farms.
options.rationale: Renewable electricity replaces fossil fuel combustion, so less carbon dioxide is emitted.

mcqs.stem: Which action would reduce emissions of methane?

options.text: Bury much more waste in landfill so that the gas cannot escape.
options.rationale: More buried waste means more decay and more methane.

options.text: Fit filters to the power station chimneys to trap the methane.
options.rationale: Filters are assumed to remove any gas, and power stations are the wrong source.

options.text: Collect the gas from landfill sites and burn it as a fuel.
options.rationale: Capturing the gas stops methane escaping into the atmosphere, and it is put to use as a fuel.

options.text: Burn less coal in the power stations that are nearby.
options.rationale: Coal is a carbon dioxide source, so the wrong gas is targeted.

mcqs.stem: Give one reason why actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions may be limited.

options.text: There is no evidence for the warming.
options.rationale: The scientific case is denied instead of a practical limit being given.

options.text: Alternative technologies cost a lot.
options.rationale: Cost is a named reason why action is limited.

options.text: Emissions cannot be measured at all today.
options.rationale: Uncertainty is turned into an inability to measure anything.

options.text: Peer review forbids any change of fuel.
options.rationale: Peer review is imagined as a rule that blocks action.
